title: Java Threads
learningObjectives: Explain a thread as an independent path of execution.
Create a task with Runnable and start a Thread.
Distinguish start from directly calling run.
Use join to wait for a thread to finish.
Recognize shared-state race conditions and synchronization needs.

understand.concept: A thread is a path of execution within a process. Java can run multiple threads concurrently. Define a task with Runnable and pass it to a Thread, then call start to schedule a new thread. Calling run directly is an ordinary method call on the current thread. Shared mutable data can create race conditions, so coordination and synchronization are needed when threads access the same state.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic equips Java learners to write robust programs using java threads in real applications.
understand.analogy: Think of each language feature as a clearly labelled tool: choose it for the specific problem it is designed to solve.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the Java language and library contracts; compile and test the actual behaviour.

explain.narrative: Prefer Runnable to separate a task from the thread that runs it. Thread.start may return before the task completes; join waits for that thread to finish. Thread scheduling is controlled by the runtime and operating system, so output order between concurrent tasks is not guaranteed unless coordination establishes an order. Avoid tests that depend on a particular scheduling sequence.

examples.title: Start a Runnable task
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("Task running")); t.start(); t.join(); System.out.println("Main finished"); } }
examples.explanation: join ensures the task completes before main prints its final line.

examples.title: Use a Runnable class
examples.code:
class MessageTask implements Runnable { public void run() { System.out.println("Hello from task"); } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread t = new Thread(new MessageTask()); t.start(); t.join(); } }
examples.explanation: A class can implement Runnable and provide its run method.

examples.title: Check thread state after join
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread t = new Thread(() -> {}); t.start(); t.join(); System.out.println(t.getState()); } }
examples.explanation: After join returns for a completed thread, its state is TERMINATED.

examples.title: Name a thread
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()), "worker-A"); t.start(); t.join(); } }
examples.explanation: A thread can be given a name for diagnostics.

examples.title: Run directly versus start
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName())); t.run(); } }
examples.explanation: Calling run directly does not create a new thread; it executes on main.

questions.prompt: Which method starts a new thread of execution?
questions.explanation: start asks the runtime to begin a new thread and invoke its run method.

questions.answer: Waits for a thread to finish
options: Waits for a thread to finish
questions.explanation: join blocks the calling thread until the target thread terminates.

questions.prompt: What happens when run is called directly?
questions.answer: It runs as a normal call on the current thread

questions.prompt: Which interface is commonly used to describe a task?
